title: Source follower
description: A source follower (common-drain buffer): the drain sits at VDD, the source drives the load, and the output tracks the input one gate-source drop below it. The voltage gain $A_v = g_m/(g_m + g_{ds} + 1/R_L)$ is just under unity and the output resistance is about $1/g_m$, so this stage buffers a high-impedance node into a resistive load $R_L$ without voltage gain. The DC level shift is one $V_{GS}$: $V_{out} = V_{in} - V_{GS}$. $V_{GS}$ is not known before sizing, so vgs_est places the operating point and the level-shift-consistent guardrail checks it against the reported $V_{GS}$; retune vgs_est until green. The body is assumed tied to the source ($V_{SB} = 0$), so no body effect appears and $g_{mb}$ drops out of the gain. That is an assumption about the layout, not an algebraic convenience: it requires an isolated body — a deep-n-well NMOS, or the PMOS-in-its-own-well version of this stage. On a bulk-grounded device the source-body generator loads the source directly; measured on a sky130 tt realization at these defaults it is about 52 uS against a 240 uS $g_m$, which pulls the gain from 0.95 down to roughly 0.79 and misses the 0.85 target. In a shared well, this sheet does not describe the circuit.

params.name: V_in
params.note: input DC level; the output sits one vgs below it

params.name: R_L
params.note: load resistance at the source; may be large (a light load approaches Av -> gm/(gm+gds))

params.name: gm_id
params.note: higher gm/ID raises gm (gain closer to 1, lower Rout) at the cost of headroom

params.name: vgs_est
params.note: estimate of the follower vgs, used to place the drain-source bias VDD - V_out; retune until the level-shift-consistent guardrail is green. The shipped value is self-consistent on the demo table; a table with a different threshold wants a different value — on a sky130 tt nfet at these defaults the guardrail lands near 0.77 — and reporting that gap is exactly what the guardrail is for

rows.name: V_out
rows.note: the DC level shift: the output is one gate-source drop below the input

rows.name: Av
rows.note: follower gain, below unity; gmb is absent because the body is tied to the source. On a bulk-grounded device it belongs in the denominator alongside gds, and costs roughly a sixth of the gain

rows.name: Rout
rows.note: output resistance, about 1/gm for a light load

rows.name: vn_in
rows.note: input-referred channel thermal density; the near-unity gain passes it through with little change

rows.name: cgg_in
rows.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents — this stage's gate capacitance. The table carries the TOTAL gate capacitance with no gate-drain split, so nothing here can weight the two terminals by how much each one swings. The drain sits at the supply, so there is no Miller multiplication to miss here; what there is instead is bootstrapping — the source follows the gate to within a few percent, taking most of $C_{GS}$ out of the driver's way, so this row OVERSTATES what the driver sees. No rule reads it

rows.name: I_q
rows.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — the one branch these rows model, set by the bias source under the follower. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no rule reads it

rules.note: gm/ID cannot exceed the weak-inversion ceiling of the data
device saturated: the drain-to-source voltage is VDD minus the source (output) level
computed from the gamma-model floor; this table carries no measured noise; the simulator owns noise sign-off

the stage is actually buffering only while the load it drives is well above its own output resistance. Ten to one is the convention for that regime, not physics: at exactly ten to one the loaded gain still sits within about ten percent of what an unloaded follower would give, and below it the load, not the device, sets the gain
the biasing vgs_est should match the reported vgs; retune it if this trips
